title: How to reverse engineer games and put them into Unreal Engine?
author: Salt_Mastodon_6422
selftext:
Hi everyone,

I’m trying to understand the practical workflow for reconstructing a compiled game as an editable, playable Unreal Engine 5.8 project.

I currently use REA with Codex to inspect game files and binaries, extract assets and available data, and study gameplay systems. I then try to reconstruct locomotion, combat, animation transitions, and other behavior in Unreal. I’m not claiming to have recovered the complete original source code.

My main question is: how do you bridge the gap between extracted assets and a working reconstruction that behaves like the original?

In particular:

* For games originally built with Unreal, how much of the cooked maps and Blueprint logic can realistically be recovered into an editable project?
* How do you approach native C++ gameplay code? Do you reconstruct it from decompiler output, or implement new systems based on observed behavior?
* For games built with another engine, is this effectively an engine reimplementation or a port?
* How do you recover the connections between animations, hit detection, effects, AI, and gameplay events?
* How do you validate that your reconstruction actually matches the original?

My immediate goal is to study these systems from inside an editable project. Longer term, I want to apply what I learn to an original game, with appropriately licensed assets and code.

Are there documented projects that have achieved this beyond asset extraction? I’d appreciate examples, practical workflows, and an honest assessment of what remains manual or cannot reliably be recovered.

replies.author: MrUnoDosTres
replies.body: I've made a PS2recomp with Codex. But since I hated how slow it was. I switched to Claude Code. And now I'm trying to turn it into a full PC port. It works, but I'm not sure if I will release it publicly though. I think Anthropic mainly makes an issue out of it when you apply this on new games. The game I'm working on is 20 years old. The only times Claude made an issue out of things was based on the licenses, but that was more like a warning. And I make it write prompts for Codex, once it gave it the task to "break" the code. Which simulated a Windows attack, which OpenAI doesn't like since its behavior was mimicking harmful software and stopped Codex. lol

comments.author: AvonMexicola
comments.body: Well sometimes is can be hard, depends on what game you are trying to make in Unreal 5.8. I am remaking wing commander 3 and they used a completely made up measurement system so I actually used 1 asset as a standard and then took a fixed distance in ingame units from that asset and measured its with in pixels. I then repeated that with every asset ingame. For speed I simply times how long it took to pass the hero asset. For the rest I just asked to decompile of find the info I needed and then rebuild it in Unreal 5.8. my game is a mod so it still requires the original gamefiles.

comments.author: Niconame
comments.body:
I don't understand what possible purpose this can have other than theft. 

Games are not that unique, if you want to port something to another stack you use traditional methods i.e. regression tests and inspecting code you have access to. 

If you want to learn to apply this to games you have appropriate license for, assets and code, you would look at open source games/projects, not try to reverse engineer the binaries.

Lastly if you want understand how to recreate game mechanics there are infinite amounts of resources, GDC talks etc where developers openly share at least the abstracts of how to implement or think about game-dev problems, so again there is no reason to go down this route.

comments.author: fisj
comments.body: I'm leaving this up despite multiple reports. We don't have a rule here (yet), and the OP doesn't obviously seem to have bad intentions. Though I do personally think they'd be better served studying open source projects to better understand professional game software development architecture.

comments.author: fisj
comments.body:
I'm actually going to comment here (not as a mod). There's a real dearth of knowledge on how to actually build games the right way. Always has been, and youtube videos rarely actually go into the meat of best practices for games software development (and often actually make it worse).

I think AI can really help here. I suggest telling a frontier model (like opus 5.5) what game you want, and ask it to do a lot of research on precedent for how your game should be built. Don't just accept it's word, co-work with it to learn about game architectures, understand why some are better for different types of games.

I suggest saving some transcripts from git-amend on youtube for various development paradigms and feeding them into your agent. Nail down the best foundation for your game. It might take a while. Also when you're planning the implementation, its best to have two different models critique and review the plans. I've had good results with opus 5.5 using Astra as a spec reviewer.

Also have an AI go through documentation and APIs for architectures, plugin and systems you'd like it to learn from and emulate. Frontier models dont need RE at this point.

My 2 cents.

comments.author: MrUnoDosTres
comments.body: I'm pretty sure you need something like Ghidra and based on for whatever console this is, some additional libraries specifically for that console.
